title: Pharmacokinetics and Initial Bolus Dosing of Furosemide in Children on ECMO.
abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is an established technology that provides life-saving mechanical support for critically ill children. In these children, fluid overload is commonly treated with furosemide; however, optimal dosing of furosemide is unknown in children supported with ECMO because ECMO may alter furosemide exposure. In this work, human blood-primed ex vivo experiments quantified red blood cell partitioning and extraction of furosemide by the ECMO circuit. Furosemide partitioned into red blood cells but was not extracted by ECMO circuits. These data then parameterized a pediatric physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model of furosemide in children with and without ECMO. Next, plasma furosemide concentrations from 10 critically ill children supported by ECMO were used to evaluate PBPK model performance, with the optimized model achieving average fold error and absolute average fold error of 1.02 and 1.67, respectively. The optimized PBPK model also predicted that ECMO increases apparent volume of distribution by a median of > 30% in neonates and infants. Finally, population PBPK simulations with the optimized PBPK model provided initial bolus doses that most rapidly achieve steady-state plasma furosemide concentrations with and without ECMO. These calibrated initial bolus doses achieved steady-state plasma furosemide concentrations > 3 h faster than continuous infusions without an initial bolus dose, and this improvement was most pronounced in neonates and infants on ECMO. Overall, this work supports comparatively larger initial bolus doses for neonates and infants on ECMO, and provides calibrated initial bolus doses based on plasma exposure for critically ill children.

title: Molecular epidemiology and genotype-based assessment of possible inter-ward spread of Acinetobacter baumannii strains in a Romanian county hospital.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii is a WHO critical-priority pathogen. Without sequencing, transmission is judged from low-resolution typing and admission records. AIM: To compare A. baumannii isolates in a Romanian county hospital by low-cost gel-based typing, test their robustness to gel sizing, and examine how admission-date sources affect the epidemiological picture. METHODS: Thirteen isolates from four departments (October-December 2024) were tested by Vitek 2 and typed by multiplex PCR of eight VNTR loci on agarose gels. As bands could not be assigned to loci, band patterns were compared (Dice, UPGMA) under 25 gel-sizing assumptions. Stays reconstructed from ward records were compared with laboratory admission dates. FINDINGS: All isolates were resistant to amikacin, ciprofloxacin, both carbapenems and tobramycin; nine (69%) were colistin-resistant by broth microdilution. One group of five isolates was separated from seven of the other eight under every sizing assumption; the eighth, and finer distinctions, were sizing-dependent. Of ten patient pairs sharing a ward, two clustered together (one with matching patterns) and seven were separated under every assumption. Laboratory admission dates lagged hospital admission in five patients. With laboratory dates the isolates formed two periods with no shared inpatient day; with reconstructed stays the periods overlapped, through one pair with matching patterns and a long-term resident whose isolate clustered with no earlier one. CONCLUSION: Some band-pattern differences persisted under every sizing assumption; whether the method can separate related from unrelated strains, and so help exclude transmission, remains to be established. Laboratory admission dates should be checked against ward-movement records.

abstract: This prospective randomized multicenter study evaluates whether the decision to prescribe antifungals guided by (1,3)-β-D-glucan in comparison to standard of care shortens time to antifungal therapy and reduces mortality in patients with severe sepsis or septic shock and a high risk of invasive candida infection.

title: MP101 in Adults With Acute Pseudomonas Aeruginosa Pneumonia
abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety and tolerability of a single intravenous dose of MP101 administered in addition to standard antibiotic therapy in adult patients with acute Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia. The study will also assess the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic characteristics of MP101 and its antibacterial activity, including changes in P. aeruginosa burden in sputum and changes in susceptibility to MP101 and concomitant antibiotics.

abstract: The purpose of this study is to compare treatment with olorofim versus treatment with AmBisome® followed by standard of care (SOC) in patients with IFD caused by proven IA or probable lower respiratory tract disease Aspergillus species (invasive aspergillosis, IA).

title: Natural History of Individuals With Immune System Problems That Lead to Fungal Infections
sourceName: National Institutes of Health Clinical Center (CC)
abstract: Background: \- The immune system is made up of special cells, tissues, and organs that fight infections. Problems with this system may lead to frequent, severe, or unusual fungal infections. These infections are often difficult to treat. Researchers want to collect blood and tissue samples from people who have unusual, persistent or severe fungal infections or immune problems that increase the risk of these infections. Objectives: \- To collect medical information and samples for a long-term study of people with immune system problems that lead to fungal infections. Eligibility: * People with a history of fungal infections caused by immune system problems. * Parents, children, and siblings of this group. * Healthy volunteers not related to the first two groups. Design: * This long-term study may last for up to 25 years. Those in the study may need to provide new information about every 6 months. The procedures for each person may vary with the particular diagnosis and the extent of fungal infection. Healthy volunteers may have only one or two visits. * At the first visit, those in the study will have a full medical history and physical exam. They will also provide blood. * Research procedures may include the following: * Saliva, urine or stool testing * Mouthwash collection for DNA testing * Collection of cheek cells, nail clippings, or vaginal fluid * Tests of leftover tissue or body fluid from previous medical procedures * Skin or oral mucous membrane biopsy * Collection of white blood cells * Followup visits will involve a physical exam and updated medical history. Blood, saliva, urine, or nail clipping samples may be taken for ongoing studies. Any additional tests or exams required by the study doctors may also be done. * Participants may withdraw from the study pool at any time.

title: Completion Pneumonectomy for Tuberculous Destroyed Lung Complicated by Aspergillosis
abstract: * Tuberculous destroyed lung remains a major indication for surgical intervention in high TB-burden regions. * Aspergillosis complicating residual cavities increases the risk of massive hemoptysis and recurrent infection. * Completion pneumonectomy is often the only curative option, but it carries significant morbidity and mortality. * Evidence is limited, and this study aims to provide structured data on perioperative and long-term outcomes.

title: CONTinuous Infusion Versus Intermittent Dosing of ceftaZidime/AVIbactam in Critically Ill Patients
abstract: Ceftazidime/avibactam (CZA) is an essential treatment option for managing infections caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) gram-negative (G-) bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae OXA-48 and carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Critically ill intensive care unit (ICU) patients frequently exhibit altered pharmacokinetics (PK) of CZA, potentially compromising optimal PK/pharmacodynamic (PD) target attainment with standard dosing regimens. This study compares the efficacy of continuous infusion (CI) versus conventional intermittent dosing (ID) of CZA in critically ill ICU patients with severe infections caused by K. pneumoniae OXA-48 or P. aeruginosa. This single-centre, randomized, open-label trial will be conducted at a tertiary care hospital within the University Hospital Centre in Zagreb, Croatia, with a 1:1 allocation ratio. One hundred forty critically ill ICU patients requiring CZA treatment will be randomized to receive either ID (2 g/0.5 g every 8 hours over 2 hours) or an equivalent dose in CI (6 g/1.5 g continuously over 24 hours). The primary outcome is the microbiological success rate. Secondary outcomes include clinical success rate, time to symptom improvement, length of ICU and hospital stay, 28-day all-cause mortality, pathogen recurrence rate, time to weaning from mechanical ventilation, cumulative vasoactive-inotropic score, adverse events, and the ratio of ceftazidime plasma concentration to the pathogen's minimum inhibitory concentration (C/MIC). This trial seeks to provide evidence on the optimal administration strategy for CZA in critically ill ICU patients with severe infections due to MDR G- pathogens.

title: P3 Study to Assess Efficacy and Safety of Cefepime/Nacubactam and Aztreonam/Nacubactam Versus Best Available Therapy for Adults With Infection Due to Carbapenem Resistant Enterobacterales
abstract: This study is a multi-center, randomized, single-blind, parallel-group study to assess the efficacy and safety, when nacubactam is coadministered with cefepime or aztreonam, compared with best available therapy (BAT), in the treatment of patients with cUTI, AP, HABP, VABP, and cIAI, due to Carbapenem Resistant Enterobacterales.

title: Pseudomonas & Pf Phage - Tobra vs Cipro
abstract: The goal of this clinical trial is to evaluate whether Pf bacteriophage (phage) status can be used as a predictive biomarker to guide antibiotic selection and improve treatment response in adolescents and adults with cystic fibrosis and chronic Pf phage-positive Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infection. Participants must be at least 12 years of age and have chronic P. aeruginosa infection with detectable Pf bacteriophage in sputum. The main questions it aims to answer are: * Does treatment with oral ciprofloxacin result in greater improvement in lung function (FEV1) than inhaled tobramycin in participants with Pf phage-positive P. aeruginosa infection? * Can Pf phage status predict clinical and microbiologic response to antibiotic therapy, including changes in bacterial density, airway inflammation, and respiratory symptoms? Researchers will compare inhaled tobramycin and oral ciprofloxacin in a randomized crossover design to determine whether participants with Pf phage-positive infection respond better to an antibiotic that is not predicted to be sequestered by Pf phage. Participants will: * Complete a 12-week randomized crossover study receiving both inhaled tobramycin and oral ciprofloxacin during separate treatment periods. * Provide sputum samples for bacterial culture, bacterial density measurements, and inflammatory biomarker analyses. * Provide blood samples for inflammatory biomarker analyses and safety monitoring * Undergo pulmonary function testing, including spirometry for measurement of FEV1 and lung clearance index measurements. * Complete quality-of-life assessments and undergo routine clinical and safety monitoring, including blood testing and anthropometric measurements.

title: Quantitative DWI-ADC metrics in extrapulmonary tuberculosis: Differentiating endemic mimics with pathological validation.
sourceName: Journal of medical imaging and radiation sciences
abstract: BACKGROUND: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) causes disproportionate morbidity due to diagnostic delays. EPTB mimics endemic infections including cryptococcal meningitis, brucellosis, and echinococcosis, creating diagnostic uncertainty. Quantitative ADC measurement offers non-invasive differentiation but population-specific cutoff values for this setting remain absent. METHODS: This prospective diagnostic accuracy study enrolled 90 adults (45 confirmed EPTB, all anti-tuberculous therapy-naive at the time of imaging, and 45 endemic disease controls) at a tertiary care hospital. PRIMARY OUTCOME: diagnostic accuracy of quantitative diffusion-weighted imaging-derived ADC for differentiating EPTB from endemic mimics. SECONDARY OUTCOMES: ADC associations with inflammatory markers; pathological correlates in surgically-confirmed cases. Standardized 1.5T/3.0T MRI protocols with quantitative ADC measurement. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. RESULTS: 90 completed (100%). TB cases: 53.3% CNS, 26.7% spinal, 20.0% abdominal; controls: 33.3% cryptococcal, 20.0% fungal, 26.7% brucellosis, 13.3% echinococcosis, 6.7% bacterial. Mean lesion ADC: TB 0.58 × 10⁻³ mm²/s versus cryptococcal 0.92, fungal 1.04, brucellosis 0.72, echinococcosis 1.18, bacterial 1.32 (p < 0.001). Optimal threshold ≤0.82: sensitivity 84.4%, specificity 88.9%, AUROC 0.919 (95% CI 0.868-0.959). ADC correlated with CSF lactate (r = -0.642) and procalcitonin (r = -0.584; both p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Quantitative ADC differentiated EPTB from endemic mimics with an AUROC of 0.919; a threshold of ≤0.82 × 10⁻³ mm²/s gave 84.4% sensitivity and 88.9% specificity, and implementation proved feasible (87.5% radiologist competency in 3.2 weeks). These estimates are provisional. The threshold was derived and evaluated in the same 90 participants without an independent test set; enrolment reached 45 cases against a calculated requirement of 64; and the cohort was drawn from a tertiary referral stream in which central nervous system and spinal disease predominated, with confirmed cases compared against confirmed alternative diagnoses rather than undifferentiated febrile presentations. The findings establish that a substantial and reproducible difference in lesion diffusivity exists, rather than accurately characterising its magnitude, and require prospective external validation before ADC-based algorithms are adopted clinically. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Tuberculosis can occur outside the lungs and can be difficult to distinguish from other infections that cause similar symptoms. This study used MRI scans from adults with tuberculosis and other infections to assess whether a measurement called the apparent diffusion coefficient, which reflects how water moves within tissues, could help tell these conditions apart. This study found that people with extrapulmonary tuberculosis had lower apparent diffusion coefficient values than those with other infections, and the measurement showed good diagnostic accuracy. This matters because a non-invasive imaging marker may help support earlier and more accurate diagnosis, although further research is needed before routine clinical use.

title: Clinical Characteristics and Prognosis of Invasive Mycosis of the Central Nervous System
abstract: This study aims to conduct a multicenter, bidirectional, observational study by enrolling patients with hematological malignancies diagnosed with CNS-IMD and receiving esconazole as first-line treatment at 12 hematological disease research centers in China from September 2022 to December 2026. The outcome measures of this study were the efficacy (all-cause mortality, fungal infection-related mortality and overall response rate) and safety (incidence of treatment-related adverse events) of initial treatment with esaconazole in patients with CNS-IMD. All-cause mortality refers to the overall mortality rate of patients at 42 days of treatment with esconazole. Fungal infection-related mortality refers to the proportion of deaths directly attributed to fungal infections. Based on clinical, imaging and microbiological results, the treatment response rates of patients at 4, 6 and 12 weeks were evaluated.

title: Assessment of [18F]-Fluorocellobiose ([18F]FCB) Pharmacokinetics in Healthy Volunteers and Subjects With Invasive Mold Infections
sourceName: National Institutes of Health Clinical Center (CC)
abstract: Background: Fungal infections can cause serious disease in the lungs and other parts of the body. About 3.8 million people die with fungal infections each year. Currently, there is no way to find fungal infections in the body using imaging scans. Researchers want to see if a new tracer (a radioactive drug that collects in certain body tissues) can help find fungal infections using positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) scans. Objective: To test a new tracer (\[18F\]Fluorocellobiose) for PET/CT scans in people with and without fungal infections. Eligibility: People aged 18 years and older who have fungal infections. Healthy volunteers are also needed. Design: Participants will have 3 clinic visits. The first visit will be for screening. Participants will have a physical exam with blood tests and a test of their heart function. The second visit will be for PET/CT scanning. A thin tube called a catheter will be inserted into a vein in the arm. The study tracer will be given through the catheter. For the scans, participants will lie on a padded bed that slides through a donut-shaped machine. The machine will take pictures of the inside of the body from the head to the upper thighs. Some participants will have only 1 scan; others will have 2 scans. The second scan will be about 90 minutes after the first one. The third visit will be for repeat blood and urine tests.

title: Etiology, Pathogenesis, and Natural History of Idiopathic CD4+ Lymphocytopenia
sourceName: National Institutes of Health Clinical Center (CC)
abstract: Background: * Idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia (ICL) is a condition in which there is a decreased level of CD4+ lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell), which can lead to opportunistic infections or autoimmune disorders and diseases. Objectives: * To characterize the natural history with regard to CD4+ T cell count and onset of infection, malignancy, and autoimmunity. * To describe the immunological status of patients affected by ICL while providing the best possible standard therapy to eradicate opportunistic infections. * To establish the timeline of CD4 lymphocytopenia, with particular focus on defining subgroups of patients according to the decline, stabilization, or rise of CD4+ T cell counts over time. * To characterize the opportunistic infections that occur in ICL patients at microbiologic and molecular levels. * To characterize the immunophenotype and possible genetic immunodeficiency causes of ICL. * To determine whether measurable immunologic parameters correlate with the development of opportunistic infections or other comorbidities such as lymphoma in patients with ICL. * To determine whether there is any association between ICL and autoimmunity. * To determine CD4+ T cell turnover, survival, functionality, and cytokine responsiveness in ICL patients. Eligibility: * Patients 2 years of age and older with an absolute CD4 count less than 300 in children 6 years or older and adults or less than 20% of T cells in children younger than 6 on two occasions at least 6 weeks apart. * Patients with negative results of HIV testing by ELISA, Western Blot, and viral load. * Patients must not have underlying immunodeficiency conditions, be receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy (anti-cancer drugs that kill cells), or have cancer. Design: * At the initial visit to the National Institutes of Health, the following evaluations will be conducted: * Personal and family medical histories. * Physical examination, including rheumatology evaluation and other consultations as medically indicated (e.g., dermatology, pulmonology, ophthalmology, imaging studies). * Blood samples for analysis of red and white blood cell counts, liver function, immune hormones, and antibody and autoantibody levels, white blood cell growth and function, and DNA. * Urinalysis and urine pregnancy testing for female patients of childbearing age. * Evaluation and treatment of active infections as medically indicated, including biopsies, buccal swabs, pulmonary function tests, and imaging studies. * Follow-up visits will take place approximately every 12 months or more frequently if indicated, and will continue for a minimum of 4 years and a maximum of 10 years. * Evaluations at follow-up will include blood samples (i.e., CBC with differential, biochemical profile, HIV testing, etc.) and urinalysis and rheumatology consults.

title: The PRECISION Partners Platform (P3) Study
abstract: Infections of the lungs are the most common problem for people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF), but also are significant in people with other lung conditions known generally as chronic suppurative lung diseases (CSLD), which can also cause recurrent chest infections. Some of the most common and severe infections are caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), Staphylococcus aureus (Sa), and Aspergillus fumigatus (Af). It is important to detect these early, in order to treat them and prevent damage to the lungs. At the moment sputum culture or cough swabs are relied upon, however, some people (for example small children or those with less severe disease) are not able to provide sputum, and cough swabs are less accurate. Additionally, although modulators such as Kaftrio and Ivacaftor have had significant positive effects on most people with CF taking them, these people often find they no longer produce sputum, and therefore testing for infections is unable to be done in the same way as before. Studies have shown that although some people have fewer infections after starting modulators, they generally don't disappear altogether, and therefore a reliable way to test for them is still needed. Furthermore, some people react differently to certain infections, and people with more than one infection simultaneously, also respond differently to these infections. The investigators would like to find new, reliable, easy and acceptable ways of testing for infections that does not require sputum and are acceptable for patients in order to detect, monitor and treat lung infections early. Additionally, the investigators would like to better understand what causes the differing responses patients have to infections, in order to see if there are new ways target treatments. The study is being undertaken in multiple centres across the UK in order to recruit a larger, more diverse and representative group of participants, than would be able to be achieved from one centre alone.

title: The antioxidant mitoquinone potentiates polymyxin activity against multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae via dual targeting of membrane phospholipids and fatty acid biosynthesis.
abstract: There is an urgent need for strategies to counter antimicrobial resistance (AMR), especially among carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE). In this study, MitoQ's potential to be utilized as a polymyxin adjuvant was explored. MitoQ alone potently inhibited Gram-positive bacteria (MICs 1-4 µg/mL) but showed weak activity against Gram-negative strains (MICs ≥ 16 µg/mL). When combined with polymyxins, MitoQ acted via a dual-target mechanism to enhance killing and reverse resistance in Enterobacteriaceae. In susceptible strains, MitoQ bound inner-membrane phospholipids, phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and cardiolipin (CL), synergizing with polymyxin-mediated outer-membrane disruption to rapidly compromise membrane integrity. In resistant strains carrying phoQ/pmrB mutations or mcr-1, membrane targeting alone did not restore sensitivity. Instead, DARTS (Drug Affinity Responsive Target Stability) methodology identified FabH, the key enzyme in the type II fatty acid synthesis (FASII) pathway, as a direct MitoQ target. Inhibition of FabH by MitoQ shifted lipid composition, decreasing saturated-to-unsaturated fatty acid ratios, and increased membrane fluidity, thereby resensitizing bacteria to polymyxins. In murine peritonitis and abscess models, co-administration of MitoQ and polymyxin B achieved > 90% reductions in bacterial load and bioluminescence compared to monotherapy. These results demonstrate that MitoQ restores polymyxin efficacy through combined membrane lipid disruption and FabH inhibition, highlighting its potential as an adjuvant to combat multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae.

title: Low-dose Liposomal Amphotericin B for Antifungal Prophylaxis in Prolonged Neutropenia Patients
sourceName: Haikou Affiliated Hospital of Central South University Xiangya School of Medicine
abstract: This is a single-center, single-arm, observational clinical study evaluating the efficacy and safety of low-dose liposomal amphotericin B (50 mg/day, intravenous, once daily) for the prevention of invasive fungal infections in adult patients (aged 18-75 years) with hematological malignancies who develop prolonged neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count ≤0.5×10\^9/L, expected to last \>7 days) and are at high risk for invasive fungal disease. Participants are those who, per the treating physician's routine clinical decision, have been initiated on liposomal amphotericin B prophylaxis at 50 mg/day due to intolerance or toxicity to other antifungal agents. The primary outcome is the incidence of proven or probable invasive fungal disease. Secondary outcomes include incidence of pneumonia, persistent unexplained fever \>4 days, use of additional systemic antifungal therapy, and adverse events. A total of 30 participants will be enrolled. Data will be collected at baseline, during treatment, and within 7 days after treatment completion.

title: Mortality and prognostic factors in invasive aspergillosis: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Invasive aspergillosis remains a life-threatening infection, but robust real-world mortality estimates are scarce. We aimed to generate contemporary overall and subgroup-specific mortality estimates for invasive aspergillosis using individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis. METHODS: In this systematic review and IPD meta-analysis, we searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science for articles published between Jan 1, 2015, and Dec 31, 2024, that reported mortality of at least ten patients with invasive aspergillosis diagnosed using established criteria, with clearly defined and analysed follow-up periods. Corresponding authors were contacted to obtain IPD on demographics, underlying conditions, site of invasive aspergillosis, diagnostic certainty, and mortality. The primary outcome was overall all-cause mortality at 4, 6, 12, and 24 weeks, 1 year, and 2 years after invasive aspergillosis diagnosis. Secondary outcomes were intensive care unit (ICU) mortality and in-hospital mortality. One-stage IPD meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled mortality. This study was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42025621772). FINDINGS: 16 020 articles were identified, of which 9686 articles were screened after removal of duplicates. Of the articles screened, 209 studies including 15 357 patients were eligible. IPD were obtained from 46 studies, comprising 3880 patients. Across IPD cohorts, patients were predominantly middle-aged and had pulmonary involvement, and probable invasive aspergillosis was the most common diagnostic certainty; classic immunocompromised host factors were common in the mortality-after-invasive aspergillosis-diagnosis cohort, whereas COVID-19 predominated in the ICU mortality cohort. Estimated overall mortality was 26·7% (95% CI 21·0-38·2) at 4 weeks, 32·0% (26·9-42·6) at 6 weeks, 41·7% (34·9-55·1) at 12 weeks, 48·5% (41·4-61·4) at 24 weeks, 53·8% (46·8-64·0) at 1 year, and 57·2% (49·7-68·3) at 2 years. ICU mortality was 57·1% (47·5-66·5) and in-hospital mortality was 46·7% (39·4-54·1). By underlying condition, estimated 4-week mortality was highest among patients with ICU admission (42·9%, 30·4-53·2). By site, estimated 4-week mortality was 27·2% (21·3-40·0) for pulmonary, 21·1% (15·1-28·9) for sinus, and 40·4% (35·0-54·5) for brain invasive aspergillosis. The overall pooled estimates yielded I INTERPRETATION: Mortality among patients with invasive aspergillosis remains high despite modern diagnostic and therapeutic advances. Greater vigilance, earlier diagnosis, and timely antifungal treatment are needed, particularly for patients with newly recognised host factors, including ICU admission and COVID-19. title: Charcot-Leyden crystals drive a localized inflammatory niche around mucus plugs in Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis.
sourceName: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
abstract: RATIONALE: Mucus plugging causes airflow obstruction, morbidity, and mortality in chronic respiratory diseases. Charcot-Leyden crystals (CLCs), formed from eosinophil-derived Galectin-10, are frequently observed in pathologic mucus, but their role in disease is unclear. OBJECTIVES: To define the prevalence, inflammatory context, and functional role of CLCs in mucus plugs, using acute allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) as a model of eosinophilic muco-obstructive disease. METHODS: Airway samples from 19 patients with acute ABPA and 61 disease controls were analyzed for CLCs and Galectin-10. Paired samples from plugged and unplugged bronchial mucosal biopsies defined the spatial relationship between CLCs and inflammation. A novel mouse model demonstrated the contribution of CLCs to airway obstruction and inflammation and enabled evaluation of CLC-directed imaging and therapy. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Airway CLCs were a sensitive and specific marker of acute ABPA. CLC-containing mucus plugs were surrounded by a localized type 2 inflammatory niche, alongside eosinophils, neutrophils and extracellular traps, whereas inflammation was minimal in unplugged airways from the same patients, or plugs lacking CLCs. In mice, CLC-containing plugs induced persistent airway obstruction and local inflammation, both reduced by a crystal-dissolving anti-Galectin-10 antibody. Galectin-10 concentrations provided a quantitative biomarker of acute ABPA, while a CLC-targeted positron emission tomography tracer enabled noninvasive visualization of crystal-rich plugs. CONCLUSIONS: CLC-containing mucus plugs form focal inflammatory niches in acute ABPA, and experimental CLC deposition is sufficient to promote persistent airway obstruction and inflammation. These findings identify CLCs as a biomarker, imaging target, and tractable therapeutic target in eosinophilic muco-obstructive airway disease.

title: A Phase 3 Efficacy and Safety Study of Fosmanogepix for the Treatment of Adult Participants With Candidemia and/or Invasive Candidiasis.
abstract: The purpose of this clinical trial is to learn about the safety and effects of the study medicine (called Fosmanogepix) for the potential treatment of candidemia and/or invasive candidiasis, a life-threatening fungal infection caused by several species of yeast called Candida. The study is seeking patients who have a diagnosis of candidemia and/or invasive candidiasis. Two-thirds of all patients will receive the study medication fosmanogepix Intravenous (IV) infusion followed by optional fosmanogepix tablets. One-third of all patients will receive a standard of care regimen of caspofungin Intravenous (IV) infusion followed by optional fluconazole capsules. Fosmanogepix or caspofungin will first be given as an Intravenous (IV) infusion directly into a vein in the arm each day at the study clinic. Fosmanogepix tablets or fluconazole capsules will be taken orally by mouth daily either at the study clinic, or at home if patients are well enough to be discharged from the hospital. The treatment effect in patients receiving fosmanogepix to those receiving caspofungin/ fluconazole will be compared. The primary aim is to show that fosmanogepix is not inferior (not worse) to caspofungin/ fluconazole with a noninferiority margin of 15%. The duration of study treatment and number of study visits will vary depending on how long the patient will be treated for the infection. Treatment will continue for a maximum of 6 weeks depending on when the infection is cleared and whether other symptoms related to the infection have improved. There will also be a follow-up visit 6 weeks after the study treatment was stopped.

title: Study of Posaconazole Prophylaxis in Patients Receiving Hematopoietic Stem Cell Allograft (Allo-HSC) at High Risk of Invasive Fungal Infection (IFI)
abstract: Patients receiving an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (allo-CSH) are at high risk of infection, particularly of fungal origin. Until the 2018 recommendations of the 6th European Conference on Infections in Leukemia (ECIL6), primary prophylaxis of invasive fungal infections (IFI), in allograft patients, was based on the administration of fluconazole until D100. Due to changes in transplantation practices (alternative donor transplantation, sequential transplantation, etc.) and changes in microbiological ecology (increased incidence of IFIs caused by filamentous germs such as aspergillosis and mycormycosis), fluconazole prophylaxis is now sometimes suboptimal. It is therefore recommended that patients at high risk of developing IFIs should be given azole molecules with activity against filamentous agents as primary prophylaxis during the first 3 months after transplantation. Posaconazole is often under-dosed (below the minimum effective concentration). It therefore seems essential to carry out a prospective study with close \[C\]min dosing in the specific situation of allograft patients, a population that appears to be at risk of underdosing in the light of initial retrospective analysis results.

title: A Phase 3 Efficacy and Safety Study of Fosmanogepix for the Treatment of Adult Patients With Invasive Mold Infections.
abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fosmanogepix (administered IV or oral) for the treatment of adult patients with invasive mold infections. title: Pharmacometrics, Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning in Precision Dosing and Clinical Toxicology.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) enables individualized pharmacotherapy for drugs with high interpatient variability and concentration-dependent effects. Conventional Bayesian approaches, although clinically established, may not fully capture pharmacokinetic complexity in dynamic or heterogeneous patient populations. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning methods offer complementary capabilities, including modeling nonlinear relationships and integrating high-dimensional clinical data. METHODS: Peer-reviewed studies that applied AI or machine-learning methods to TDM between January 2017 and April 2026 were reviewed in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. Studies involving adult and pediatric populations were included, whereas reviews, editorials, and animal studies were excluded. RESULTS: Forty-seven studies covering a range of drugs, including vancomycin, tacrolimus, antiepileptics, mycophenolic acid, methotrexate, and voriconazole, were included. Tree-based ensemble methods, particularly eXtreme Gradient Boosting, random forest, and gradient boosting, were the most frequently applied algorithms. In general, these methods demonstrated strong predictive performance, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values up to 0.90 for classification tasks and coefficient of determination values up to 0.85 for regression tasks. In 13 studies, AI models demonstrated predictive performance comparable with or exceeding that of traditional population pharmacokinetic and Bayesian approaches for selected applications. However, these comparisons were heterogeneous and often based on retrospective data sets with limited external validation. CONCLUSIONS: AI-based methods have considerable potential for enhancing TDM, particularly for dose optimization, drug-exposure estimation, and toxicity prediction. However, evidence linking improved predictive performance to meaningful clinical outcomes remains limited.

title: Clinicobacteriological profile, Mortality Predictors and Antimicrobial Resistance in Necrotising Soft Tissue Infections: A prospective study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Necrotising soft tissue infections (NSTIs) are rapidly progressive infections requiring prompt diagnosis and management. This study assessed predictors of mortality, microbiological spectrum, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and differences between polymicrobial and monomicrobial NSTIs in a prospective manner. METHODS: This study enrolled patients aged 15 years or older with clinically suspected NSTIs who presented between March 2022 and February 2023. Clinical, laboratory, surgical, and outcome data were collected. Tissue and pus samples were processed for aerobic and anaerobic cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI guidelines. Mortality-associated factors were analysed using univariate analysis, binary logistic regression, and survival analysis. RESULTS: Eighty-seven patients were included, predominantly male (87.3%), with a median age of 47.5 years. Extremities were most commonly affected. The mortality rate of this cohort was 25.3%. Polymicrobial infections predominated (49.4%), while monomicrobial NSTIs were associated with higher mortality (p = 0.022). Gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii and Escherichia coli, were the most frequent pathogens. Obligate anaerobes were significantly associated with polymicrobial infections. Chronic liver disease (p = 0.003) and systemic toxicity (p = 0.018) independently predicted mortality, whereas higher haemoglobin levels were protective. High antimicrobial resistance was observed, including carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and Enterobacterales. Among the anaerobes, resistance to clindamycin and cefoxitin, along with reduced susceptibility to metronidazole, was reported. CONCLUSION: NSTIs remain associated with substantial mortality, especially in monomicrobial infections due to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Early recognition, prompt surgery, and region-specific empirical antimicrobial therapy are crucial for improving outcomes.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis of therapeutic drug monitoring and CYP2C19 genotyping for voriconazole in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study assessed the clinical outcomes and economic impact of voriconazole therapy guided by therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) combined with CYP2C19 genotyping for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). METHODS: We analysed retrospective data from patients with COPD and treated with voriconazole for IPA at a large comprehensive tertiary hospital in western China from 2022 to 2025. Propensity score matching (PSM) was applied to balance covariates and compare outcomes between the TDM plus CYP2C19 genotyping group and the control group. Primary endpoints included fungal treatment response rate and adverse drug events (ADEs) incidence rate. A decision-tree model was used to evaluate the quality-adjusted life years (QALY) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER). Robustness was tested through one-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses, including Monte Carlo simulation. RESULTS: Of 249 patients, 142 were included after PSM (71 in each group). The overall response rate was significantly higher in the TDM plus CYP2C19 genotyping group than in the control group (64.79% versus 47.89%, P = 0.042), with no significant difference were observed in the incidence of ADEs (P = 0.956). Cost-effectiveness analysis indicated that TDM plus CYP2C19 genotyping is cost-effective, providing greater health benefits (QALYs = 0.5859, incremental QALYs = 0.0168), with an ICER of 21 610.71$ per QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis showed that at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $41 859 per QALY, the probability of TDM plus CYP2C19 genotyping being cost-effective was 72.0%. CONCLUSION: Patients receiving TDM plus CYP2C19 genotyping-guided voriconazole treatment exhibited higher clinical response rates in this PSM-matched real-world IPA complicated COPD cohort. Within the preset parameter assumptions and 1-year decision-tree framework of this economic model, the combined regimen demonstrated favourable cost-effectiveness outcomes.

title: A literature-informed pharmacokinetic framework for polymyxin B dosing during continuous renal replacement therapy: integrating renal function and extracorporeal clearance.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Existing population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) models for polymyxin B in patients receiving CRRT remain limited, and all of them have neglected the impact of membrane materials on drug adsorption. Recently, a few studies have attempted to construct integrated PK models by combining pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters derived from patients not receiving CRRT with CRRT-specific parameters. However, current integrated models only consider non-renal clearance and CRRT clearance (CLCRRT), excluding residual renal function (RRF). This study aimed to construct a literature-informed PK framework for polymyxin B incorporating intrinsic clearance (CLintrinsic, adjusted by CrCL to account for RRF) and CLCRRT, with CLCRRT comprising transmembrane (CLTM) and adsorptive (CLads) components. METHODS: CLCRRT allocation was set to 0% CLads for the PS membrane and 100% CLads for the AN69 membrane. The frameworks predictive performance was evaluated using two literature datasets (n = 53 and n = 30) and a prospective cohort (n = 10). Simulation analyses used PTA ≥90% as the criterion for adequate pharmacodynamic target attainment and a simulated probability of AUC RESULTS: The framework demonstrated accurate predictions of polymyxin B exposure in patients not receiving CRRT and those receiving CRRT (prediction error <30%). Filter type was the primary determinant of drug exposure, exceeding the effects of RRF or CRRT intensity. For the PS membrane (AV600S filter) and MIC = 0.5 mg/L pathogens, doses should be stratified based on CrCL with standard or lower doses. For the AN69 membrane (OXIRIS filter), a high-dose regimen (200 mg LD + 150 mg MD q12h) should be considered for infections with an MIC of 0.5 mg/L. DISCUSSION: These findings suggest that filter type and RRF should be considered when individualizing polymyxin B dosing during CRRT. The proposed framework and the Shiny application are intended as research tools and require prospective clinical evaluation and therapeutic drug monitoring before routine clinical use.

abstract: BACKGROUND: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health crisis, yet regional disparities remain poorly characterized. abstract: BACKGROUND: Candida species are major causes of fungal infections worldwide, and non-albicans Candida species (NAC) pose increasing clinical challenges due to changing epidemiology and antifungal resistance. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate the species-distribution and antifungal susceptibility profiles of clinical Candida isolates collected in the Taiwan Surveillance of Antimicrobial Resistance of Yeasts (TSARY) survey in 2022. Species identification and susceptibility testing against amphotericin B, anidulafungin, fluconazole and voriconazole were performed. All voriconazole-resistant isolates were also cross-resistant to fluconazole. CONCLUSIONS: The present study highlights increasing fluconazole resistance in C. tropicalis and the continued detection of rare yeast species with potential clinical significance in Taiwan, supporting the importance of continuous surveillance, accurate identification and updated susceptibility monitoring.

Patients who developed postoperative BSI were identified and a 1:1 propensity score matched analysis were performed to adjust for baseline characteristics of patients. Univariate and multivariate analysis were applied to identify independent risk factors for postoperative BSI. R software was used to construct a prediction nomogram, followed by internal validation. RESULTS: During the study, a total of 10,007 patients underwent heart surgery, and 164 pairs of patients were successfully matched using propensity score matching. Gram-negative bacteria were the most common pathogens (64.1%), followed by Fungi (18.2%) and Gram-positive bacteria (17.6%). Among CONCLUSION: Postoperative BSI in cardiac surgery patients is associated with high mortality. A nomogram based on impaired cardiac function (NYHA II-IV), pulmonary infection, emergency surgery, CABG, CRRT and postoperative ICU stay ≥14 d displayed high accuracy and consistency in predicting the risk of postoperative BSI. These results facilitate early risk stratification and guide preventive strategies in high-risk cardiac surgical patients.

title: Targeted Antimicrobial Comparison for Treatment Individualization in Critically Ill Patients With CRAB Infection
abstract: The goal of this prospective, multicenter observational study is to learn which antibiotic treatment strategies are associated with better outcomes in critically ill adults with severe infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB). The study will also evaluate the safety and costs of different treatments and develop prediction models to support personalized treatment decisions. The main questions it aims to answer are: Are there differences in 28-day survival between patients receiving polymyxin-based and non-polymyxin-based antibiotic treatments? Which treatment strategies are associated with better clinical recovery, bacterial clearance, and fewer adverse events, particularly acute kidney injury? Can clinical data and machine learning help predict treatment outcomes and support safer, more effective treatment decisions? Researchers will compare patients receiving polymyxin-based combination therapy with those receiving non-polymyxin-based treatments, including high-dose sulbactam-based, tigecycline-based, and newer antibiotic regimens. Treatment decisions will be made by the patients' treating physicians as part of routine clinical care, rather than assigned by the researchers. Participants will: Receive antibiotic treatments determined by their treating physicians. Have clinical information collected during hospitalization, including laboratory tests, bacterial cultures, organ function, antibiotic use, adverse events, and medical costs. Be followed for 28 days after starting targeted antibiotic treatment to assess survival and clinical outcomes. title: Bronchoscopic phenotypes and anatomical airway involvement in invasive tracheobronchial aspergillosis without classic immunosuppression: association with in-hospital mortality.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The prognostic relevance of visual bronchoscopic phenotyping and airway lesion extent in invasive tracheobronchial aspergillosis (ITBA) without classic immunosuppression remains unclear. This study aimed to describe the clinical, radiological and bronchoscopic features of ITBA, and to evaluate the association between visual bronchoscopic assessment and in-hospital mortality. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at National Lung Hospital in Hanoi, Vietnam, from January 2023 to December 2025. Adult patients with histopathologically proven ITBA lacking classic immunosuppressive factors were included. On bronchoscopy, patients were dichotomised by the predominance of pseudomembranes and an airway involvement score was calculated to assess the extent of the lesions. RESULTS: The study included 31 patients with proven ITBA (mean age 61.4 years; 83.9% male). Diabetes (41.9%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (29.0%) were the most common comorbidities, and 16.1% of the cohort were immunocompetent. Bronchoscopy revealed the pseudomembranous phenotype in 61.3% of patients. Overall in-hospital mortality was 29.0%. Beyond the diagnostic utility, bronchoscopy may provide prognostic relevance for this selected cohort, particularly through evaluation of the anatomical extent of airway involvement, rather than visual bronchoscopic phenotyping.

title: Multidrug-resistant Candida auris osteomyelitis treated with fosmanogepix and surgical source control: A report of a case with favorable outcome.
abstract: Candida auris is an emerging fungus that can cause serious infections in hospitalized patients. It is especially concerning because it is often resistant to several of the medicines normally used to treat fungal infections. Bone infections caused by Candida auris are very rare, and there is little information to guide treatment when the organism is resistant to multiple antifungal drugs. We describe the case of a 44-year-old woman with a chronic pressure sore complicated by a severe infection involving the hip and femur caused by a highly drug-resistant strain of Candida auris. The fungus was resistant to the standard antifungal medications typically used for Candida infections. Candida auris was repeatedly recovered from deep surgical specimens, including bone, despite initial treatment and surgical debridement. Successful management required repeated surgical removal of infected bone and soft tissue, followed by reconstruction and careful wound management. Because there were no suitable approved antifungal options, the patient also received fosmanogepix, a newer antifungal medication provided through a special access program. She completed six weeks of fosmanogepix therapy, which was given as part of a combined treatment approach that included three surgical debridements and definitive wound reconstruction. At the end of antifungal therapy, the wound was continuing to heal and there were no clinical signs of active infection. Healing continued after treatment was stopped, and no recurrence was identified during 12 months of follow-up. This case highlights the importance of aggressive surgical source control in the management of Candida auris osteomyelitis and suggests that fosmanogepix may have a role as part of a combined medical and surgical approach when standard antifungal therapies are not suitable. Further studies are needed to better define the effectiveness, optimal duration, and role of fosmanogepix in bone and joint infections.

title: Anti-MDA5-associated rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease in clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis with secondary invasive pulmonary Aspergillus flavus infection after aggressive immunosuppressive therapy: a case report.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Anti-melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) positive rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) with clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (CADM) is a life-threatening condition. Prompt initiation of immunosuppressive therapy is crucial for improving outcomes. However, such treatment strategies substantially increase the risk of opportunistic infections, including invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA), even in patients without typical risk factors. CASE PRESENTATION: A 59-year-old previously healthy woman reported a four-month history of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and hoarseness, initially treated as pneumonia without clinical improvement. On admission, the patient presented with tachypnea, hypoxemia, bilateral crackles, and Gottron papules but no muscle weakness. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) suggested organizing pneumonia, and serological testing revealed strongly positive anti-MDA5 antibodies, raising suspicion for RP-ILD associated with CADM. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid culture grew Aspergillus flavus, which was considered colonization due to non-specific imaging and absence of typical risk factors. From day 7 to day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated rapidly, with progressive respiratory failure accompanied by a marked hyperinflammatory state. Follow-up HRCT demonstrated worsening ground-glass opacities, consolidations, and traction bronchiectasis. A diagnosis of RP-ILD associated with CADM and positive anti-MDA5 antibodies was established. Aggressive triple immunosuppressive therapy was promptly initiated, including pulse methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide, and mycophenolate mofetil. Subsequently, the patient developed fever and a positive serum galactomannan assay, raising a strong suspicion of IPA. Combination antifungal therapy with amphotericin B lipid complex and voriconazole was administered. Despite these interventions, respiratory failure continued to worsen, necessitating mechanical ventilation. The patient died on day 17 of hospitalization due to acute respiratory distress syndrome and septic shock. CONCLUSION: This case highlights the dual challenge of managing anti-MDA5-associated RP-ILD and recognizing opportunistic infections during intensive immunosuppression. IPA may occur as a life-threatening complication caused by A. flavus, even in the absence of classical risk factors or typical radiological features, leading to delayed diagnosis. Routine screening for IPA using serum or bronchoalveolar lavage galactomannan should be considered in patients undergoing potent immunosuppressive therapy.

title: Maribavir pharmacokinetics during in vitro continuous renal replacement therapy.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Maribavir is a well-tolerated option for drug-resistant CMV, though there is no available guidance for dosing in patients on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). This study aimed to determine maribavir clearance and hemofilter adsorption during CRRT to inform dosing recommendations. METHODS: Maribavir pharmacokinetic profiles were quantified using an in vitro model. Total clearance during CRRT (CLCRRT) in addition to sieving (SC), and saturation (SA) coefficients were calculated based on these experiments. Optimal maribavir doses were then estimated from the in vitro parameters. RESULTS: The mean SA was 0.853 and did not differ by filter type (P = 0.831). The SC was higher with the M150 filter (0.102) than for the HF1400 filter (0.080; P = 0.040). Across all experiments, the mean maribavir CLCRRT ranged from 0.19 to 0.49 L/hr and did not significantly differ between continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) and continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD) (P = 0.853) but was higher at 4 vs. 2 L/hr (P = 0.007). The mean CLCRRT was lower with the M150 filter compared to the HF1400 filter (P = 0.063), which was attributed to the higher adsorption with HF1400. Filter type and effluent flow rate were independently associated with CLCRRT for CVVH whereas only effluent flow rate was independently associated with CLCRRT for CVVHD. The package insert dose of 400 mg twice daily would lead to adequate concentrations across the most common flow rates (1-4 L/hr) with either modality or filter type. CONCLUSIONS: Maribavir clearance during CRRT was relatively low, though it adsorbed significantly more to the HF1400 filter. At typical CRRT flow rates, standard dosing of 400 mg twice daily is predicted to provide adequate exposures.

title: A Clinical Trial of Resistant Potato Starch for Gut MDRO Decolonization

abstract: Multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) cause serious infections that are difficult to treat, leading to increased morbidity and mortality, longer hospital stays, and increased healthcare costs. Many risk factors for MDRO infections are present in the Veteran population (such as older age, underlying medical conditions like diabetes, and stays in long-term healthcare settings). Some people can carry these organisms in their gut. Even without current symptoms, carrying these MDROs also increases risk of future infection. Effective, easy to use, and inexpensive interventions to reduce gut carriage of MDROs are needed to reduce risk of infection. Dietary fiber prebiotics have shown promise in improving the healthy gut microbiome, and the investigators have found that individuals with high fiber in their diets have reduced carriage of MDROs in the gut. The investigators propose a randomized controlled trial to test the effectiveness of a dietary fiber prebiotic intervention (resistant potato starch) in reducing gut MDRO carriage in Veterans with a history of MDRO carriage and/or infection. The investigators will also evaluate the effect on the gut microbiome as well as Veterans' experience with the fiber intervention.

title: Association between severe RSV pneumonia and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) is a life-threatening opportunistic infection, most often seen in severely immunocompromised patients. In patients without classical host factors such as neutropenia, IPA has been described in critically ill patients with influenza and COVID-19. In past years, associations between IPA and other respiratory viruses have been made, especially in immunocompromised hosts. In our institute, we have recently observed multiple critically ill patients with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and IPA, mostly in patients who had undergone allogeneic hematological stem cell transplantation (HSCT). We evaluated the prevalence and potential risk factors of IPA in critically ill patients with an RSV infection. METHODS: In a retrospective cohort study between January 1st 2016 and December 31st 2024 patients who had been admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for respiratory support and underwent a bronchoalveolar lavage that was positive for RSV of whom clinical information was available, were included. Data regarding underlying disease, radiology, mycological tests, and mortality were analyzed. RESULTS: We identified 16 ICU patients that received respiratory support due to an RSV pneumonia. Of these, five patients (31%) had probable IPA, all of whom had undergone an allogeneic SCT. The 30-day mortality of IPA in these patients was 100%. Patients with an allogeneic HSCT and severe RSV had increased prevalence of IPA compared to RSV negative patients, albeit non-significantly (56% vs. 23%, p = 0.10). CONCLUSIONS: IPA associated with RSV appears to occur limited to post-allogeneic HSCT recipients and carries a dismal prognosis.

title: Outbreak-driven dissemination of KPC variant-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae: the emerging challenge of ceftazidime/avibactam and cefiderocol co-resistance.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ceftazidime/avibactam (CZA) resistance in KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae is a critical public health threat, traditionally associated with in vivo selection. In this three-year study conducted in an Intensive Care Unit (ICU), we aimed to investigate the emergence of CZA-resistant (CZA-R) K. pneumoniae in patients treated with CZA, assessing the possible role of hospital outbreaks in dissemination. METHODS: We analysed a three-year dataset of antibiotic consumption and K. pneumoniae isolates collected from ICU patients receiving CZA therapy. Whole-genome sequencing (Illumina/Oxford Nanopore) and epidemiological reconstruction were used to investigate resistance mechanisms, KPC variants, and transmission dynamics, including outbreak detection. RESULTS: Among 871 ICU patients, 17.9% received CZA therapy, and 9% of these tested positive for CZA-resistant strains. We identified eight distinct KPC variants, including the novel KPC-295. While in vivo evolution remained the primary driver (71.4%), epidemiological reconstruction revealed that 28.6% of resistant isolates resulted from horizontal transmission, forming three distinct outbreaks of KPC-31, KPC-62, and KPC-66 producers. Alarmingly, 76.2% of CZA-R isolates exhibited co-resistance to FDC, a phenomenon linked to the presence of KPC variants conferring CZA resistance and likely enhanced by the fec operon. These clones persisted in the hospital environment and gut reservoirs of CZA-naive patients. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that CZA-R outbreaks may be underreported due to difficulties in KPC variant diagnostics and outbreak reconstruction. The emergence of co-resistance to CZA and FDC severely limits treatment options and poses major challenges for patient care and antimicrobial stewardship. These findings underscore the need for strengthened infection prevention and control measures, including early microbiological detection, active surveillance, and prompt containment strategies in ICU settings.

Global genomic surveillance and temporal trends of carbapenemase-encoding β-lactamase genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae using NCBI pathogen detection data.
abstract: The global spread of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is weakening the effectiveness of last-resort antibiotics and making severe infections increasingly difficult to treat. This study examined the geographical distribution, temporal patterns and co-occurrence of carbapenemase genes among K. pneumoniae genome assemblies deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information Pathogen Detection database. Genome metadata and antimicrobial resistance genotype information were retrieved between January and February 2026. After data cleaning, 67,057 unique genome assemblies from 123 countries contributed 77,975 carbapenemase-gene detections. Gene frequencies were summarised by continent, country, year and sample source. Poisson and negative binomial regression models were used to examine temporal patterns from 2013 to 2025. Genome-level co-occurrence was assessed using phi correlation coefficients, Jaccard similarity, odds ratios and Fisher's exact tests. blaKPC was the most frequently detected gene, with 39,832 detections (51.08%), followed by blaNDM with 24,412 (31.31%). blaNDM was the dominant gene in Africa, accounting for 1,101 detections (52.68%), whereas blaKPC was dominant in the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania, accounting for 59.29%, 56.50%, 38.37% and 38.77% of detections, respectively. Urine and blood were the main sample sources, representing approximately 30% and 22% of the analysed genomes, respectively. Yearly trend analysis showed increases in blaNDM, blaOXA-232 and blaOXA-181. The strongest negative association was found between blaKPC and blaNDM (φ = -0.69), although genomes carrying either gene frequently contained additional antimicrobial resistance genes. These findings demonstrate clear geographical and temporal differences in carbapenemase genes among genome assemblies deposited in NCBI pathogen detection. However, differences in sequencing capacity and database submissions across countries and years should be considered when interpreting the findings. Continued genomic surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship and stronger infection prevention and control measures are needed, particularly in underrepresented regions.

title: Respiratory fungal colonization in hospitalized patients in western Iran: species distribution and antifungal susceptibility patterns.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Respiratory fungal colonization is frequently observed among hospitalized patients with underlying pulmonary disorders; however, its clinical significance, species distribution, and local antifungal susceptibility patterns remain incompletely characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This study aimed to determine the frequency of culture-confirmed fungal detection in respiratory specimens, describe the distribution of fungal species, assess antifungal susceptibility profiles of predominant isolates, and examine associations between culture positivity and selected demographic and clinical characteristics in western Iran. METHODS: This prospective cross-sectional observational study was conducted over a 12-month period (July 2020-July 2021) at two tertiary-care hospitals in western Iran. A total of 127 consecutive respiratory specimens, including sputum (with quality assessment using Bartlett criteria), bronchoalveolar lavage, and tracheal aspirates, were examined by direct microscopy and fungal culture. Fungal isolates were identified using a combination of conventional phenotypic and molecular methods. CHROMagar, germ tube testing, and carbohydrate assimilation profiling were applied exclusively to yeast isolates, while filamentous fungi were identified using phenotypic methods and confirmed by ITS rDNA sequencing for representative isolates. Antifungal susceptibility testing of predominant isolates was conducted using CLSI broth microdilution methods (M27 A4 for yeasts, M38 A2 for filamentous fungi). MICs were interpreted using CLSI species-specific breakpoints or epidemiological cutoff values where available; for Candida glabrata, fluconazole MICs were categorized as Susceptible Dose-Dependent (SDD), and for Aspergillus species, isolates were categorized as wild-type (WT) or non-wild-type (NWT) based on ECVs. Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. RESULTS: Fungal growth was detected in 62 of 127 respiratory specimens (48.8%). Yeasts constituted the majority of isolates (71.0%). Candida albicans was the most frequently identified species (37.1%), followed by C. glabrata (17.7%), C. tropicalis (9.7%), and C. parapsilosis (6.5%). Among filamentous fungi, Aspergillus flavus was the most commonly isolated mold (9.7%), followed by Rhizopus spp. (6.5%), A. fumigatus (4.8%), A. niger (4.8%), and Penicillium spp. (3.2%). Culture positivity was highest in sputum specimens (51.9%), followed by bronchoalveolar lavage (44.4%) and tracheal aspirates (33.3%); however, these differences were not statistically significant (p = 0.19). No significant associations were found between culture positivity and demographic or clinical variables, including age, sex, COPD, pneumonia, malignancy, diabetes mellitus, or COVID-19 status; however, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited sample size. C. albicans isolates exhibited high susceptibility to the tested antifungal agents (with MIC₅₀ and MIC₉₀ values of 0.5 and 2 µg/mL for fluconazole), whereas elevated fluconazole MICs (with 36.4% of isolates categorized as SDD) were observed among C. glabrata isolates. All A. flavus isolates tested were categorized as wild-type for amphotericin B and voriconazole based on CLSI ECVs. CONCLUSIONS: Culture-confirmed fungal detection was common in respiratory specimens from hospitalized patients with suspected lower respiratory tract disorders. Yeasts, particularly Candida species, predominated, while A. flavus was the leading mold isolate, reflecting regional epidemiological patterns. The high proportion of Candida isolates should be interpreted with caution, as recovery of Candida from respiratory secretions almost always represents colonization rather than infection and should not routinely prompt antifungal therapy in non-neutropenic patients. No significant associations were observed between culture positivity and the evaluated clinical variables, although this may be attributable to the limited sample size and incomplete data on clinically relevant risk factors such as ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and corticosteroid exposure. These findings emphasize the need for cautious interpretation of respiratory fungal culture results, species-level identification, and antifungal susceptibility testing as components of antifungal stewardship. Larger multicenter studies with comprehensive risk factor assessment, fungal biomarkers, and longitudinal follow-up are needed to clarify the clinical significance of respiratory fungal colonization and its potential progression to invasive disease.

title: Fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic critically ill patients: a Delphi consensus from the Fungal Infection Study Forum, India, with implications for resource-limited settings.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop consensus-based, pragmatic recommendations for the diagnosis and management of fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic critically ill adults in India and Asia, where the dual burden of mucormycosis and resource-limited healthcare settings creates distinct challenges. METHODS: Using a modified Delphi process, 20 multidisciplinary experts participated in the first round, and 19 completed the second and third rounds of anonymous voting on risk factors, diagnostic strategies, and management of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA), pulmonary mucormycosis (PM), and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). Consensus was defined as ≥ 70% agreement or disagreement; statements with 60-69% agreement were categorized as "suggest," while the remaining were classified as "no consensus." RESULTS: Key risk factors included severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, influenza, COVID-19, diabetes mellitus, and chronic liver or kidney disease. A multimodal diagnostic strategy combining contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), early bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), microscopy, culture, and galactomannan (BAL threshold ≥ 1.0) was recommended, with molecular methods used where available. Liposomal amphotericin B was the preferred empiric agent in regions with high mucormycosis prevalence; voriconazole, posaconazole, or isavuconazole are first-line for proven IPA. Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for azole antifungals, with a minimum treatment duration of 6-12 weeks. For PCP, empiric trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is recommended in immunosuppressed patients with diffuse ground-glass opacities on CT after exclusion of competing diagnoses. Adjunctive corticosteroids are recommended for PCP with severe hypoxemia (PaO₂ <70 mmHg) despite limited evidence in non-HIV patients. CONCLUSION: We provide practical, resource-adapted guidance for managing fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic ICU patients, while highlighting research priorities. The proposed diagnostic criteria for IPA and PM are provisional consensus-based frameworks intended to support clinical decision-making and require prospective multicentre validation.
